t: Darius the Great had the text carved on a cliff above the road between Babylon and Ecbatana. It gives his ancestry, lists the lands he ruled and recounts nineteen battles fought in one year against rebels and impostors.
It is the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription, written in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, and this made it important to the decipherment of cuneiform.

Forgotten for centuries and explained in fanciful ways, it was copied by travellers and scholars from 1598 onward, and Henry Rawlinson sent a full and accurate copy of the Old Persian text to Europe in 1847.
dyk: Darius's beard on the relief is a separate block of stone attached with iron pins and lead, and one of the nine bound figures appears to have been added after the others were finished.
ev: Darius was crowned king of the Achaemenid Empire in the summer, and the rebellions that the inscription describes followed the death of Cambyses II
Darius fought nineteen battles in a period of one year, ending in December, to put down the rebellions
Robert Sherley saw the inscription on a diplomatic mission to Safavid Persia and brought it to the attention of Western European scholars
Pietro della Valle visited the inscription and made preliminary drawings
Carsten Niebuhr visited the site and published a copy of the inscription in 1778
Henry Rawlinson began studying the inscription in earnest and later scaled the cliff to copy the Old Persian text
Rawlinson sent a full and accurate copy of the Old Persian inscription to Europe
The site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site

f.made: Authored by Darius the Great, king of the Achaemenid Empire, sometime between his coronation in the summer of 522 BCE and his death in autumn 486 BCE
f.form: A rock relief and trilingual cuneiform inscription in Old Persian, Elamite and Babylonian, about 15 metres high and 25 metres wide: 414 lines in five columns in Old Persian, 260 lines in eight columns in Elamite and 112 lines in Babylonian
f.where: On a limestone cliff at Mount Behistun (Bisotun), near Kermanshah in western Iran, about 100 metres above an ancient road between Babylon and Ecbatana; an Aramaic copy of the text was found in Egypt
f.known: the longest known trilingual cuneiform inscription; the key to deciphering Old Persian cuneiform; Darius's account of his ancestry and of nineteen battles in a year; the list of twenty-three subject lands; the relief of Darius and the bound rebels; Henry Rawlinson's climb to copy it; UNESCO World Heritage listing in 2006
